prompt: What does a heatmap keep from the table it is drawn from?

choices.text: Its rows and columns, and their order
choices.why: Right. Colour replaces the numbers; the structure stays.

choices.text: The exact value of every cell, readable by eye
choices.why: Shading is at the bottom of the ladder; exact values need numbers.

choices.text: The order of the rows by value
choices.why: A heatmap keeps whatever order the table has, sorted or not.

choices.text: Nothing; it is a different kind of chart
choices.why: It is the table, with colour doing the first reading.

prompt: Which data suits a heatmap best?

choices.text: Orders by region and month
choices.why: Right. Two category or step axes, one quantity in the cells.

choices.text: Delivery time against distance for 400 deliveries
choices.why: Two continuous quantities make a scatterplot.

choices.text: The share of revenue in each of three categories
choices.why: One axis of three categories wants bars, or one pie.

choices.text: One region's orders over 24 months
choices.why: A single series over time is a line.

prompt: A spreadsheet offers a red, yellow and green colour scale first. Why is it the wrong choice for counts of orders?

choices.text: Spreadsheets cannot print red
choices.why: They can; the issue is meaning, not printing.

choices.text: Three colours are too few
choices.why: The problem is not the number of colours.

choices.text: Green always means bad
choices.why: Green usually means good, which is part of the problem: it says good or bad where counts are neither.

choices.text: Counts only go up, so one hue from pale to dark fits
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12 explains it in full.

prompt: The week heatmap has seven days and the hours from 8:00 to 22:00. How many cells does it have?
Why is every cell on the diagonal of a correlation matrix 1.00?

choices.text: Each is a variable with itself
choices.why: Right, which is why those cells carry no information.

choices.text: The diagonal holds the strongest pairs
choices.why: The strongest real pairs sit off the diagonal.

choices.text: The values were rounded up
choices.why: Nothing was rounded; a variable always correlates perfectly with itself.

choices.text: It marks the variables with the largest numbers
choices.why: Correlation does not depend on the size of the numbers.

prompt: A correlation matrix of 6 variables has how many distinct pairs, not counting a variable with itself?
The correlation between two variables is 0.03. What can you conclude?

choices.text: The two are unrelated in every way
choices.why: Correlation only sees straight lines.

choices.text: One causes the other weakly
choices.why: Correlation says nothing about cause.

choices.text: There is no straight-line relationship; a curved one is still possible
choices.why: Right. Draw the scatterplot before concluding there is nothing.

choices.text: The data has errors
choices.why: Low correlations are common and usually correct.

prompt: Items and basket correlate at 0.95. A colleague proposes dropping basket from a report because it adds nothing. What is the strongest reply?

choices.text: 0.95 means basket causes items
choices.why: Correlation says nothing about which causes which.

choices.text: Correlations above 0.9 are usually errors
choices.why: Here it is exactly what was expected: more items cost more.

choices.text: He is right; they are the same variable
choices.why: They are different units, items and reais, and the 5% that differs can matter.

choices.text: Close is not identical; reais still matter
choices.why: Right. A strong correlation means they move together, not that one replaces the other in money.

prompt: Should the rows of the week heatmap, Monday to Sunday, be sorted by total orders?

choices.text: No, the days keep their order
choices.why: Right. Days have their own sequence and readers need it.

choices.text: Yes, the busiest day first
choices.why: That breaks the week the reader is looking for.

choices.text: Yes, alphabetically
choices.why: Alphabetical order breaks the week as well.

choices.text: Only if weekends are moved to the top
choices.why: Any reordering of days hides the weekly rhythm.

prompt: After the correlation matrix was reordered, what did the two strong pairs become?

choices.text: Two dark blocks along the diagonal
choices.why: Right. Related variables now sit side by side.

choices.text: Two dark cells in opposite corners
choices.why: That was closer to the file's order, before reordering.

choices.text: A single dark row
choices.why: A dark row would mean one variable correlated with everything.

choices.text: Pale cells, because the values changed
choices.why: Reordering moves cells; it never changes a value.

prompt: Why must the rows and columns of a correlation matrix use the same order?

choices.text: Software refuses different orders
choices.why: It will draw them; the result is just unreadable.

choices.text: So the diagonal stays a diagonal and the mirror stays a mirror
choices.why: Right. Different orders scatter the ones and break the symmetry.

choices.text: To keep the variables in alphabetical order
choices.why: The order should group related variables, not follow the alphabet.

choices.text: Because correlations are always positive
choices.why: They can be negative, and this has nothing to do with sign.

prompt: What is a dendrogram, drawn along the edge of a clustered heatmap?

choices.text: The colour legend
choices.why: The legend is the scale of values.

choices.text: A histogram of each row's values
choices.why: That would be a distribution, not a tree.

choices.text: A line of totals for each column
choices.why: Totals are sometimes added, but they are not a dendrogram.

choices.text: A tree of which rows were joined first
choices.why: Right. It shows the grouping that produced the order.

prompt: Why write the number inside each heatmap cell?

choices.text: To make the cells look fuller
choices.why: Decoration is not the reason.

choices.text: Colour shows where; the number shows what
choices.why: Right. Shading cannot tell 147 from 150.

choices.text: Because the colour scale is optional then
choices.why: Keep the scale: it says what dark means.

choices.text: So the chart can be printed in black and white
choices.why: That is a side benefit, not the main one.

prompt: Which colour scale fits a correlation matrix?

choices.text: Diverging, pale at zero
choices.why: Right. Zero means no relationship, a meaningful middle.

choices.text: Sequential, from pale at −1 to dark at +1
choices.why: That would make −0.9, a strong relationship, look like nothing.

choices.text: A rainbow from red to violet
choices.why: Hue has no order, so the reader cannot tell which colour is stronger.

choices.text: One colour for every cell, with numbers only
choices.why: Then the colour does no reading at all.

prompt: In an annotated heatmap, all the numbers are drawn in dark grey. What goes wrong?

choices.text: They make the pale cells look darker
choices.why: Text does not change how the cell reads.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as they have two decimals
choices.why: Decimals do not help text the reader cannot see.

choices.text: They vanish on the darkest cells
choices.why: Right. Dark cells need light text; the contrast decides, cell by cell.

choices.text: Grey numbers suggest the values are estimates
choices.why: Readers do not read colour of text that way; the problem is contrast.

prompt: Why draw only half of a correlation matrix?

choices.text: Half the correlations are negative
choices.why: The sign does not decide which half is drawn.

choices.text: The other half mirrors it
choices.why: Right. Half the cells repeat the other half.

choices.text: The upper half is less accurate
choices.why: Both halves hold the same numbers.

choices.text: To leave room for a legend
choices.why: There are better reasons, and the legend fits either way.

prompt: In this heatmap the rows are Monday to Sunday from the top and the columns are 8:00 to 22:00 from the left. Find each of these.

labels.text: the busiest hour of the week

prompt: The tree drawn along the edge of a clustered heatmap, showing which rows were joined first, is a ___.
Put the steps of building a readable correlation heatmap in order.
items: Compute the correlation of every pair
Reorder the variables so related ones sit together
Colour the cells on a diverging scale centred at zero
Write each value in its cell and keep half the matrix
